summary: micro-G is a dashboard over the 24 combustion investigations of NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, for researchers and engineers who work on fire safety in crewed spacecraft and habitats. It addresses the Flame in Freefall challenge by ordering the investigations by how directly they bear on fire safety, giving one card per investigation in which every statement carries the literal passage of the PSI record it comes from, and publishing a per-test table of the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) that can be downloaded. A user describes a situation in a crewed habitat in microgravity (what can burn and in which phase, and whether the concern is to prevent, detect or suppress a fire) and gets the findings of the matching investigations, with their citations. It matters because the conditions and results of these investigations are spread across long text records and test files; the dashboard puts what each one found next to its source, so that whoever designs a mission or an experiment can check it. This project is not affiliated with NASA and is not endorsed by it.
details:
What it does. The dashboard answers one question: given a concrete situation in a crewed habitat in microgravity, which fire risks have to be considered according to the fire-safety investigations in PSI, and which results on the physics of flames in microgravity support them? It answers with what each investigation found, with its citation. It has four views:

- Catalog. The 24 investigations in three levels that the team assigned by hand: fire safety (12), physical basis (8), and efficiency and propulsion (4). The reason for each one is in data/levels.csv. Within a level, the investigations with per-test tables come first.

- Investigation card. A fixed set of fields per investigation. Each field shows the passage of the PSI record it comes from; what the record does not say is shown as "Not stated in source".

- Situation. The user describes a situation with selectors (fuel phase, pillar and phenomenon) and gets the findings of the matching investigations, fire-safety studies first and the physics that supports them after.

- Quantitative data. One row per FLEX test, 271 rows read from the 272 test sheets in PSI, with a chart of the measured points and a CSV download.

What it does not do. It does not assess risk and does not order anything by level of risk: the PSI records give neither probability nor severity. It does not recommend safety measures and does not generate scenarios; that judgment belongs to whoever designs the mission or the experiment. It does not match a situation by atmosphere (oxygen, pressure, flow), because most PSI records do not report those conditions. It does not fit any relation over the FLEX table: the table is published as read from the sheets.

How it works. A snapshot of the 24 PSI records and their file listings is taken without credentials. Before publishing, a language model drafted each card into a fixed schema, with the literal passage behind every field. A script then checks every field against the PSI record: the passage has to appear literally in the field it names, and every number in the summary has to be in that passage. Only the fields that pass are published. Of 159 fields checked, 147 passed and 12 were dropped. Two team members also reviewed a sample of 30 verified fields by hand, and 27 were correct; the fields found wrong were removed. The site shows these numbers in its verification panel. No text on the site is written live by a language model.

Benefits. A researcher or engineer can see, for a given situation, which investigations bear on it and what each one found, and can open the PSI passage behind every statement. What the records do not say stays visible as a gap instead of being filled in.

What we hope to achieve. A reference that can be checked line by line against its source, for those who design missions and experiments on fire safety in microgravity.

Tools and languages. Python, standard library only, for the scripts that take the PSI snapshot, read the FLEX test sheets, build and check the cards and build the catalog. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no third-party library, for the site. Cloudflare Pages hosts the site; GitHub hosts the repository and runs a hygiene check on every change. The Gemini API drafted the cards before publishing.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI). The idea of the solution and the levels of the catalog are the team's. SI tools were used as follows, and what they produced is marked in the project:

- Claude Code (Anthropic), models claude-opus-5-5 and claude-fable-5-2. Assisted in writing the code and the documentation. Each file written with its assistance carries a header line AI-assisted: <tool> (<model>), reviewed by <github-user>.

- Claude in Chrome (Anthropic), model claude-opus-5-5. Read source pages in a browser for the team, such as license pages and the PSI passages of the manual sample; a team member checked what it returned against the pages.

- Gemini API (Google), model gemini-3.5-flash-lite, free tier. Drafted the investigation cards before publishing; only public NASA text was sent. Each card carries a generated_by field with the tool, the model and the date, and the site shows it on each card. Only the fields whose passage is found literally in the PSI record are published.

The ai-log/ folder of the repository records, per team member, what was asked, with which tool and model, and what a person checked or corrected. It also carries the mark for files that cannot hold a comment, such as JSON. No image, video or audio was generated with SI.

License. The original work of the project is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. The full table of sources, with every license page, is in the README.md of the repository, https://github.com/jofavalle/micro-g.
